sections.title: Fats
sections.narration: 12.6 grams of fat. Cholesterol is 63 milligrams, which is fairly controlled for a meat. Saturated fat is 4.36 grams though, so there is still some real baggage attached. Omega 3 is only 90 milligrams, meaning it is not bringing much of the more useful fat usually found in oily fish. For meats, the fat mix decides how cleanly the protein arrives, and pork loin lands somewhere in the middle.

sections.title: Carbs
sections.narration: 0 grams of carbs. There is no sugar, starch, or fibre to score, which is exactly what you would expect from plain pork. That makes it easy to use in a lower-carb meal, but the vegetables, beans, or grains around it still need to bring the fibre. For meats, carbs are not the job unless breading, glaze, or sauce gets added.

sections.title: Proteins
sections.narration: 19.7 grams of protein. All 9 essential amino-acid groups clear their useful amount targets, meaning the body gets the full set needed for muscle repair and maintenance. It also scores 10 out of 11 for the nonessential groups, so the wider amino-acid coverage is strong too. For meats, usable complete protein is the main job, and pork loin handles that part very well.

sections.title: Vitamins
sections.narration: Vitamin B12 is 22% daily value. B12 supports the nerves and helps make red blood cells that carry oxygen around the body. Vitamin D is only 3% daily value, while vitamins A, C, E, and K barely show up. For meats, one useful B12 result is welcome, but the overall vitamin range is still pretty thin.

sections.title: Minerals
sections.narration: Zinc is 16% daily value, giving useful support for immune function, healing, and normal hormone production. Potassium is 8% daily value, which helps a little with fluid balance and muscle function but is not especially strong. Iron is only 4% daily value, much lower than people might expect from a meat. For pork loin, zinc does most of the mineral work.

sections.title: Pros
sections.narration: The upsides first: plain loin is a world away from processed pork. It does not need curing, smoking, breading, or a mystery ingredient list to work. One roast can cover several meals. Dinner first, then sandwiches, wraps, or stir-fries with the leftovers. The mild flavour takes seasoning really well. Change the herbs, spice mix, or sauce and the same cut can go in a completely different direction.

sections.title: Cons
sections.narration: The drawbacks next: the safe-temperature rule matters. Whole pork cuts need to reach 145 degrees Fahrenheit, then rest for at least 3 minutes. Overcooking can dry it out fast. Loin is not very forgiving once it sails past the sweet spot. Some prepackaged options have salty water added. Check the label if you want plain pork without the extra salt.

closing.summary: Best bits are complete protein, strong amino-acid coverage, useful B12 and zinc, and being much less processed than bacon, sausages, or ham. Weak spots are the middling fat profile, low iron, poor vitamin range, and how easily cooking or added solutions can change the result. Best for muscle-focused meals and practical batch cooking. Add vegetables and a fibre-rich carb, use a thermometer, and do not cook the life out of it.
